claims.claim: Pitch discrimination in humans is thought to be driven by two acoustical cues that result from low-numbered 'resolved' harmonics and high-numbered 'unresolved' harmonics.
claims.source: Pitch discrimination in humans is thought to be driven by two acoustical cues that result from low-numbered 'resolved' harmonics and high-numbered 'unresolved' harmonics (Moore and Gockel, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moore and Gockel, 2011.

claims.claim: In the frequency domain, F0 can be determined from the distribution of harmonics.
claims.source: In the frequency domain, F0 can be determined from the distribution of harmonics (Figure 1A, upper panel) (Goldstein, 1973; Shamma and Klein, 2000; Terhardt, 1974).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldstein, 1973; Shamma and Klein, 2000; Terhardt, 1974, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In the auditory nerve, the frequency spectrum is represented as a 'place code' of activation across the tonotopic map as well as a 'temporal code' of spikes that are phase-locked to basilar membrane vibrations.
claims.source: In the auditory nerve, the frequency spectrum is represented as a 'place code' of activation across the tonotopic map as well as a 'temporal code' of spikes that are phase-locked to basilar membrane vibrations (Cariani and Delgutte, 1996; Schnupp et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cariani and Delgutte, 1996; Schnupp et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Both place code and temporal code representations are limited by the cochlea's frequency resolution.
claims.source: However, both these representations are limited by the cochlea's frequency resolution (Goldstein, 1973).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldstein, 1973.

claims.claim: Cochlear filter bandwidths increase with frequency.
claims.source: Because cochlear filter bandwidths increase with frequency, only low-numbered harmonics produce discernible peaks of excitation and phase locked spikes at their centre frequency (Figure 1A, middle panel).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory science, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Only low-numbered harmonics produce discernible peaks of excitation and phase locked spikes at their centre frequency.
claims.source: Because cochlear filter bandwidths increase with frequency, only low-numbered harmonics produce discernible peaks of excitation and phase locked spikes at their centre frequency (Figure 1A, middle panel).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: High-numbered harmonics produce beating in time at the F0, conveyed by phase-locking to their envelope.
claims.source: By contrast, high-numbered harmonics are not individually resolved, and instead produce beating in time at the F0, conveyed by phase-locking to their envelope (Schouten, 1970) (Figure 1A, bottom panel).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schouten, 1970 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Humans can extract F0 using either resolved harmonics or unresolved harmonics alone.
claims.source: Although psychophysical experiments have demonstrated that humans can extract F0 using either resolved harmonics or unresolved harmonics alone (Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994), human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics (Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994; Shofner and Campbell, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994.

claims.claim: Human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics.
claims.source: Although psychophysical experiments have demonstrated that humans can extract F0 using either resolved harmonics or unresolved harmonics alone (Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994), human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics (Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994; Shofner and Campbell, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994; Shofner and Campbell, 2012.

claims.claim: Marmosets can use resolved harmonics to detect F0 changes.
claims.source: Marmosets can also use resolved harmonics to detect F0 changes (Bendor et al., 2012; Song et al., 2016), whereas rodents (i.e. gerbils and chinchillas) rely more upon temporal periodicity cues (Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendor et al., 2012; Song et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Rodents (i.e. gerbils and chinchillas) rely more upon temporal periodicity cues.
claims.source: Marmosets can also use resolved harmonics to detect F0 changes (Bendor et al., 2012; Song et al., 2016), whereas rodents (i.e. gerbils and chinchillas) rely more upon temporal periodicity cues (Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009; Shofner and Chaney, 2013.

claims.claim: Species differences in perception could relate to the pitch cues that are available following cochlear filtering.
claims.source: It has been suggested that these apparent species differences in perception could relate to the pitch cues that are available following cochlear filtering (Cedolin and Delgutte, 2010; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cedolin and Delgutte, 2010; Shofner and Chaney, 2013.

claims.claim: Cochlear bandwidths are broader in many non-human species.
claims.source: In particular, the growing evidence that cochlear bandwidths are broader in many non-human species (Joris et al., 2011; Shera et al., 2002), including ferrets (Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018), supports the possibility that they might process pitch cues in different ways from humans, as has been noted previously (Shofner and Campbell, 2012; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joris et al., 2011; Shera et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Ferrets have broader cochlear bandwidths than humans.
claims.source: In particular, the growing evidence that cochlear bandwidths are broader in many non-human species (Joris et al., 2011; Shera et al., 2002), including ferrets (Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018), supports the possibility that they might process pitch cues in different ways from humans, as has been noted previously (Shofner and Campbell, 2012; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The spectral range of stimuli was not fully controlled across F0 in some previous studies.
claims.source: Second, the spectral range of stimuli was not fully controlled across F0 in some previous studies (e.g. Song et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2009), making it possible for animals to base their behavioural choices on the lower spectral edge of the sounds, rather than the sound's overall F0.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Song et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The pitch difference thresholds of ferrets can differ by orders of magnitude between a go/no-go and 2AFC task.
claims.source: For example, the pitch difference thresholds of ferrets can differ by orders of magnitude between a go/no-go and 2AFC task (Walker et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Humans are believed to have narrower cochlear filter bandwidths than ferrets.
claims.source: Humans (Glasberg and Moore, 1990; Shera et al., 2002) are believed to have narrower cochlear filter bandwidths than ferrets (Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018; Sumner and Palmer, 2012) and other non-human animals (Joris et al., 2011; Osmanski et al., 2013; Pickles and Comis, 1976), and these physiological constraints may predispose them to rely on different acoustical cues to classify the pitch of complex tones.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Glasberg and Moore, 1990; Shera et al., 2002 for humans and Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018; Sumner and Palmer, 2012 for ferrets.

claims.claim: Sharper frequency tuning in humans should result in more resolvable harmonics across the human tonotopic map.
claims.source: Specifically, sharper frequency tuning in humans should result in more resolvable harmonics across the human tonotopic map.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between cochlear filter bandwidth and harmonic resolvability.

claims.claim: Broader bandwidth of an auditory nerve fibre should result in stronger phase locking to the beating of adjacent harmonics.
claims.source: On the other hand, if the bandwidth of an auditory nerve fibre is broader, its firing should phase lock more strongly to the beating of adjacent harmonics, potentially providing a stronger explicit representation of the temporal periodicity of F0 in ferrets than in humans.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between cochlear filter bandwidth and temporal envelope representation.

claims.claim: The cochlear filters are wider for the ferret auditory nerve than the human.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1B, the cochlear filters are wider for the ferret auditory nerve than the human, even with the difference in the methods used to obtain the two sets of bandwidth estimates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Individual low-numbered harmonics of the tone are more clearly resolved in the human cochlea than in the ferret.
claims.source: When the instantaneous power of the cochlear filters is summed across the duration of the sound and plotted as a function of centre frequency, the individual low-numbered harmonics of the tone are more clearly resolved in the human cochlea than in the ferret (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The representation of the 500 Hz F0 is clearer in the ferret than in the human in the temporal domain.
claims.source: To visualize the temporal representation of the higher harmonics in the same stimulus, we plotted the output of a single nerve fibre (here, a fibre with a centre frequency of 5 kHz) throughout time (Figure 1D). In this case, the representation of the 500 Hz F0 is clearer in the ferret – the human cochlea produces weaker temporal modulation because fewer harmonics fall within the fibre's bandwidth.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The average temporal representation of F0 was enhanced in the ferret compared to the human.
claims.source: The average temporal representation of F0 was enhanced in the ferret compared to the human (Wilcoxon rank sum test; z = 8.286, p=1.175×10−16).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the cochlear model data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The F0 representation metric was higher in the ferret than the human cochlear model across every pair of individually simulated auditory nerve fibres.
claims.source: In fact, this F0 representation metric was higher in the ferret than the human cochlear model across every pair of individually simulated auditory nerve fibres.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the cochlear model data.

claims.claim: The ferret cochlea provides an enhanced representation of the envelope periodicity of a complex tone, as conveyed by spikes that are phase-locked to the F0 in the auditory nerve.
claims.source: These simulations suggest that the ferret cochlea provides an enhanced representation of the envelope periodicity of a complex tone, as conveyed by spikes that are phase-locked to the F0 in the auditory nerve.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cochlear model simulations.

claims.claim: The human auditory nerve provides a better resolved representation of individual harmonics across the tonotopic array.
claims.source: On the other hand, the human auditory nerve provides a better resolved representation of individual harmonics across the tonotopic array.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cochlear model simulations.

claims.claim: Five ferrets were trained on a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task that requires 'low' and 'high' pitch judgements.
claims.source: To test the role of different pitch cues in ferret pitch perception, we trained five animals on a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task that requires 'low' and 'high' pitch judgements analogous to those used in human psychophysical tasks (Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claims.claim: Four ferrets were trained to classify harmonic complex tones with an F0 of 500 and 1000 Hz.
claims.source: We began by training four ferrets to classify harmonic complex tones with an F0 of 500 and 1000 Hz, with a repeating pure tone presented at 707 Hz (the midpoint on a logarithmic scale) for reference before each trial.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claims.claim: Three ferrets were trained to classify harmonic complex tones with target F0 values of 150 and 450 Hz.
claims.source: Two of these animals, along with one naïve ferret, were then trained on the same task using target F0 values of 150 and 450 Hz and a 260 Hz pure tone reference.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claims.claim: The integer ratios between the F0s to be discriminated allowed exact matching of their spectral bandwidths.
claims.source: In both cases, the integer ratios between the F0s to be discriminated allowed us to match their spectral bandwidths exactly, so that ferrets could not solve the task based on the frequency range of the sound (Figure 3; first four rows).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claims.claim: The ferrets learned to perform the pitch classification task within 22 ± 3 days of twice daily training.
claims.source: After completing several pre-training stages to habituate the animals to the apparatus and sound presentation (see Materials and methods), the ferrets learned to perform the pitch classification task within 22 ± 3 (mean ± standard deviation) days of twice daily training.
claims.evidence: This is a report of experimental results.

claims.claim: The inner ear produces distortion in response to harmonic tones that can introduce energy at the fundamental frequency to the basilar membrane response.
claims.source: The inner ear is known to produce distortion in response to harmonic tones that can introduce energy at the fundamental frequency to the basilar membrane response, even for missing-fundamental sounds (Robles et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robles et al., 1991.

claims.claim: Ferrets performed more poorly on probe trials than on standard trials.
claims.source: Ferrets performed more poorly on probe trials than on standard trials (paired t-test; t = 4.346, p=0.005), as expected for an auditory discrimination task performed in noise.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferrets performed the pitch classification at 71.85 ± 9.60% correct with the noise masker.
claims.source: However, they performed the pitch classification at 71.85 ± 9.60% correct (mean ± standard deviation) with the noise masker, which is well above chance (1-sample t-test; t = 6.025, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferrets did not rely on cochlear distortion products to solve the pitch classification task.
claims.source: This suggests that ferrets did not rely on cochlear distortion products to solve our task.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing above-chance performance with noise masking.

claims.claim: The standard tones contained both resolved and unresolved harmonics for ferret listeners.
claims.source: This analysis suggests that our standard tones contained both resolved and unresolved harmonics for ferret listeners, as intended.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the auditory nerve model analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli).
claims.source: A repeated-measures 3-way ANOVA was carried out on the three ferrets trained with both references. This analysis indicated that performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli) (F(4,8) = 10.540, p=0.003), but not across subjects (F(2,8) = 1.060; p=0.391) or the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz) (F(1,8) = 0.438, p=0.576).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferret performance did not vary across subjects.
claims.source: A repeated-measures 3-way ANOVA was carried out on the three ferrets trained with both references. This analysis indicated that performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli) (F(4,8) = 10.540, p=0.003), but not across subjects (F(2,8) = 1.060; p=0.391) or the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz) (F(1,8) = 0.438, p=0.576).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferret performance did not vary across the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz).
claims.source: A repeated-measures 3-way ANOVA was carried out on the three ferrets trained with both references. This analysis indicated that performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli) (F(4,8) = 10.540, p=0.003), but not across subjects (F(2,8) = 1.060; p=0.391) or the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz) (F(1,8) = 0.438, p=0.576).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Compared to their performance on standard trials, ferrets showed impaired performance on probes that contained only low harmonics.
claims.source: To assess the acoustical cues used by animals to solve the pitch classification task, we compared ferrets' performance on the standard trials with that on each of the four probe trial types (repeated measures 2-way ANOVA, Tukey's HSD test). Compared to their performance on standard trials, ferrets showed impaired performance on probes that contained only low harmonics (p=0.001), but performed well when only high harmonics were presented (p=1.000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferrets performed well when only high harmonics were presented.
claims.source: To assess the acoustical cues used by animals to solve the pitch classification task, we compared ferrets' performance on the standard trials with that on each of the four probe trial types (repeated measures 2-way ANOVA, Tukey's HSD test). Compared to their performance on standard trials, ferrets showed impaired performance on probes that contained only low harmonics (p=0.001), but performed well when only high harmonics were presented (p=1.000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferrets' performance was impaired when the phases of the high harmonics were randomized.
claims.source: Their performance was impaired when we randomized the phases of the high harmonics (p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Phase randomization impaired ferret performance when the full set of harmonics (both resolved and unresolved; 'All Harmonics Random Phase') were present.
claims.source: Phase randomization also impaired performance when the full set of harmonics (both resolved and unresolved; 'All Harmonics Random Phase') were present (p=2.173×10−5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Ferrets rely more strongly on the temporal envelope periodicity (produced by unresolved harmonics) than on resolved harmonics to classify the pitch of harmonic tone complexes.
claims.source: This pattern of results suggests that ferrets rely more strongly on the temporal envelope periodicity (produced by unresolved harmonics) than on resolved harmonics to classify the pitch of harmonic tone complexes, unlike what would be expected for human listeners.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of behavioral results.

claims.claim: Human listeners showed varied pitch classification performance across the standard and probe stimuli.
claims.source: Human listeners also showed varied pitch classification performance across the standard and probe stimuli (repeated-measures 2-way ANOVA; F(4,60) = 36.999, p=1.443×10−15).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: A different pattern of performance across stimuli was observed for human subjects than for ferrets.
claims.source: However, a different pattern of performance across stimuli was observed for human subjects than for ferrets (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: Human listeners were significantly impaired when resolved harmonics were removed from the sounds.
claims.source: Tukey's HSD tests indicated that human listeners were significantly impaired when resolved harmonics were removed from the sounds, as demonstrated by impairments in the 'High Harmonic' probes with (p=9.922×10−9) and without (p=1.029×10−8) randomized phases.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: No impairment was observed in human listeners when resolved harmonics were available, regardless of whether the phases of stimuli were randomized or not.
claims.source: Conversely, no impairment was observed when resolved harmonics were available, regardless of whether the phases of stimuli were randomized ('All Harmonics Random Phase' condition; p=0.959) or not ('Low Harmonics' condition; p=0.101).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: While ferrets were impaired only when temporal envelope cues from unresolved harmonics were disrupted, humans continued to classify the target pitch well in the absence of temporal envelope cues, so long as resolved harmonics were present.
claims.source: Consistent with the relative prominence of the cues in our model simulations, we found that while ferrets were impaired only when temporal envelope cues from unresolved harmonics were disrupted, humans continued to classify the target pitch well in the absence of temporal envelope cues, so long as resolved harmonics were present.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results comparing the two species.

claims.claim: There was a significant interaction between species and stimulus type on performance.
claims.source: This was confirmed statistically as a significant interaction between species and stimulus type on performance (2-way ANOVA; F(4,135) = 14.720, p=5.274×10−10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The two species predominantly rely on distinct cues to pitch.
claims.source: The two species thus appear to predominantly rely on distinct cues to pitch.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results.

claims.claim: Broader cochlear filter widths in ferrets result in fewer resolved harmonics and a more enhanced representation of temporal envelopes than the human cochlea.
claims.source: Our model simulations illustrated how broader cochlear filter widths in ferrets result in fewer resolved harmonics and a more enhanced representation of temporal envelopes than the human cochlea, as suggested by previous authors (Cedolin and Delgutte, 2010; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the cochlear model simulations and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The results provide the first unambiguous dissociation of pitch mechanisms across species.
claims.source: Our results provide the first unambiguous dissociation of pitch mechanisms across species, by utilizing the same task across species, and provide an illustration of the potential consequences of species differences in cochlear tuning.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the significance of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Human listeners have consistently been found to have better pitch discrimination thresholds when stimuli contain resolved harmonics.
claims.source: Human listeners have consistently been found to have better pitch discrimination thresholds when stimuli contain resolved harmonics (Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Kaernbach and Bering, 2001; Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Kaernbach and Bering, 2001; Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994.

claims.claim: Cortical responses to pitched sound in humans are stronger for resolved than unresolved harmonics, mirroring perceptual sensitivity.
claims.source: Moreover, cortical responses to pitched sound in humans are stronger for resolved than unresolved harmonics, mirroring perceptual sensitivity (Norman-Haignere et al., 2013; Penagos et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Norman-Haignere et al., 2013; Penagos et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Humans may learn to derive pitch primarily from resolved harmonics even when temporal envelope cues are also available.
claims.source: Because most natural sounds contain both low- and high-numbered harmonics, humans may learn to derive pitch primarily from resolved harmonics even when temporal envelope cues are also available, and are thus less equipped to derive pitch from unresolved harmonics alone.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed behavioral pattern.

claims.claim: Ferrets may learn to rely more on temporal pitch cues when estimating pitch from natural sounds.
claims.source: As a result, they may conversely learn to rely more on temporal pitch cues when estimating pitch from natural sounds, leading to poorer performance for low harmonic tone complexes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed behavioral pattern in ferrets.

claims.claim: Species differences in pitch perception may be even more pronounced than suggested by the simulations.
claims.source: In fact, these species differences may be even more pronounced than suggested by our simulations, as ferret filters appear to exhibit broader bandwidths when measured with the simultaneous masking paradigms from which the human bandwidths in our simulations were obtained (Sumner et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on citation to Sumner et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Many non-human mammals are thought to have wider cochlear bandwidths than humans.
claims.source: Many non-human mammals are thought to have wider cochlear bandwidths than humans (Joris et al., 2011; Liberman, 1978; Sumner et al., 2018; Temchin et al., 2008), and so we might expect temporal cues to dominate their pitch decisions as we have observed in ferrets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joris et al., 2011; Liberman, 1978; Sumner et al., 2018; Temchin et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Studies in gerbils suggest that they primarily use temporal cues to detect an inharmonic component in a tone complex.
claims.source: For instance, studies in gerbils suggest that they primarily use temporal cues to detect an inharmonic component in a tone complex (Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009.

claims.claim: Chinchillas were shown to detect the onset of a periodic sound following a non-periodic sound using temporal, rather than resolved harmonic, cues.
claims.source: Chinchillas were similarly shown to detect the onset of a periodic sound following a non-periodic sound using temporal, rather than resolved harmonic, cues (Shofner, 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shofner, 2002.

claims.claim: Marmosets appear to be influenced by harmonic phases when detecting changes in F0 only when resolved harmonics are omitted from the stimulus.
claims.source: Marmosets, on the other hand, appear to be influenced by harmonic phases when detecting changes in F0 only when resolved harmonics are omitted from the stimulus (Bendor et al., 2012; Osmanski et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendor et al., 2012; Osmanski et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Temporal cues are only salient for marmosets when they occur in unresolved harmonics.
claims.source: This suggests that temporal cues are only salient for this species when they occur in unresolved harmonics.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cited marmoset studies.

claims.claim: Marmosets were found to detect smaller changes in F0 when harmonics were resolved than when only unresolved harmonics were available.
claims.source: Similarly to humans, marmosets were found to detect smaller changes in F0 when harmonics were resolved than when only unresolved harmonics were available (Song et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Ferrets show an order of magnitude difference in pitch acuity on F0 change detection versus F0 direction labeling tasks.
claims.source: Ferrets show an order of magnitude difference in pitch acuity on these two tasks (Walker et al., 2011), raising the possibility that primates might as well.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The results do not preclude the possibility that ferrets could also make pitch judgments based on resolved harmonics if trained to do so.
claims.source: The ferrets relied predominantly on temporal cues under these conditions, but our results do not preclude the possibility that they could also make pitch judgments based on resolved harmonics if trained to do so.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of the study's conclusions.

claims.claim: Humans can extract pitch from unresolved harmonics when they are isolated.
claims.source: Indeed, although human listeners rely on resolved harmonics under normal listening conditions, we can also extract pitch from unresolved harmonics when they are isolated (Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994.

claims.claim: Multiple harmonics could potentially be resolved on the ferret cochlea, depending on the F0.
claims.source: Our simulations show that multiple harmonics could potentially be resolved on the ferret cochlea, depending on the F0 (Figure 4A).

results.result: Pitch perception (F0) is critical for recognizing speech, music, and animal vocalizations, encoding meaning in speech and musical melody, providing cues to identity, aiding attention in noisy environments, and helping non-human animals identify individuals and interpret communication calls.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C8-C12) are well-supported by established scientific knowledge and multiple citations to prior work. They provide appropriate background context for the study and are not contested in the manuscript.

results.result: The neurobiological basis of pitch perception remains unsettled due to divergent results across species. While many mammalian species can discriminate F0, pitch acuity differs markedly across species, and the neural mechanisms underlying pitch extraction in auditory cortex are unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C13-C20 establish the scientific motivation for the study through well-cited prior work. The claims accurately represent the state of the field regarding cross-species differences and neural mechanisms of pitch perception.

results.result: Human pitch discrimination is driven by two acoustical cues: resolved harmonics (low-numbered harmonics producing discernible peaks in the tonotopic map) and unresolved harmonics (high-numbered harmonics producing temporal envelope periodicity). Human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C29 accurately describe established principles of pitch perception in humans, supported by appropriate citations and illustrated in Figure 1A. This provides essential theoretical background for the experimental work.

results.result: Prior animal studies suggest species differences in pitch cue use: marmosets can use resolved harmonics while rodents rely more on temporal cues. These differences may relate to cochlear filtering, with broader cochlear bandwidths in non-human species including ferrets. However, previous studies had methodological limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 appropriately review prior work and identify methodological gaps that motivate the current study. The citations support the claims about species differences and the limitations of previous experimental designs.

results.result: Cochlear modeling simulations demonstrate that ferrets have broader cochlear filter bandwidths than humans, resulting in fewer resolved harmonics but enhanced temporal envelope representation of F0 in ferrets compared to humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C46 are supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 1B-E, with appropriate statistical analysis (C43: Wilcoxon test, p<10^-16). The model parameters are derived from published measurements for each species, though the authors acknowledge using different measurement methods (psychophysics for humans, auditory nerve recordings for ferrets), which they note provides a conservative estimate.

results.result: Five ferrets were trained on a 2AFC pitch classification task with F0 targets of either 150/450 Hz or 500/1000 Hz. Ferrets learned the task within 22±3 days and performed above chance (71.85±9.60% correct) with noise masking, indicating they did not rely on cochlear distortion products.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C55 describe the behavioral methods and initial validation results. The experimental design appropriately controls for spectral edge cues (C50) and distortion products (C52-C55), with statistical support (C53: t=4.346, p=0.005; C54: t=6.025, p=0.001). The task design enables direct comparison with human psychophysics.

results.result: Ferrets showed impaired performance when only low (resolved) harmonics were presented (p=0.001) but performed well with high (unresolved) harmonics (p=1.000). Phase randomization impaired performance for high harmonics (p=0.002) and all harmonics (p<10^-5), suggesting ferrets rely more on temporal envelope periodicity than resolved harmonics.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (repeated measures 2-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD tests) shown in Figure 5A. The pattern of results across probe conditions provides converging evidence for the interpretation. Performance did not vary across subjects (C58) or reference conditions (C59), supporting data pooling.

results.result: Human listeners showed the opposite pattern from ferrets: they were significantly impaired when resolved harmonics were removed (p<10^-8) but showed no impairment when resolved harmonics were available regardless of phase randomization. A significant species × stimulus interaction (F(4,135)=14.720, p<10^-9) confirms the two species rely on distinct pitch cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are supported by statistical analyses and data shown in Figure 5B. The human results replicate prior work while using a task analogous to the ferret experiment, enabling valid cross-species comparison. The significant interaction (C70) provides strong statistical support for species differences.

results.result: The study provides the first unambiguous dissociation of pitch mechanisms across species using the same task. Ferrets accurately generalized pitch discriminations when temporal envelope cues were robust but not when resolved harmonics were the main cue, while humans showed the opposite pattern. These differences can be attributed to species-specific cochlear filter bandwidths.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 and C72-C73 represent the main conclusions, integrating the modeling (C6, C72) and behavioral results (C3-C5). The conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of computational predictions and empirical findings. The claim of 'first unambiguous dissociation' (C73) is justified by the use of matched tasks and appropriate controls.

results.result: The results are consistent with prior human psychophysics showing better pitch discrimination with resolved harmonics and stronger cortical responses to resolved harmonics. Humans may learn to derive pitch primarily from resolved harmonics, while ferrets may learn to rely more on temporal cues. Species differences may be even more pronounced than simulations suggest.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 appropriately contextualize results with prior work. Claims C76-C77 offer reasonable speculative explanations for the observed patterns. Claim C78 acknowledges limitations of the modeling approach, noting that ferret bandwidths from simultaneous masking would be even broader, making the conclusions conservative.

results.result: Many non-human mammals have wider cochlear bandwidths than humans, suggesting temporal cues may dominate their pitch decisions. Studies in gerbils and chinchillas support reliance on temporal cues, while marmosets appear more similar to humans in using resolved harmonics, though task differences may contribute to apparent species differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C85 appropriately discuss how the findings relate to other species, with proper citations. The discussion acknowledges task-dependent differences (C85) as a potential confound in cross-species comparisons, which strengthens the rationale for the current study's matched-task design.

results.result: The results do not preclude ferrets from using resolved harmonics if specifically trained, as humans can also extract pitch from unresolved harmonics when isolated. The relationship between harmonic resolvability and auditory nerve tuning is not fully understood. Overall, pitch judgments appear adapted to the acoustical cues available in each species.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 appropriately discuss limitations and alternative interpretations. The acknowledgment that ferrets might use resolved harmonics with different training (C86, C89) and that the relationship between resolvability and tuning is incompletely understood (C90) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. The synthesis (C91) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Ferrets can estimate F0 from temporal envelopes and generalize across sounds with different spectral properties without relying on explicit energy at F0, suggesting they have a pitch percept weighted differently than humans. Ferrets favor temporal cues even for F0s as high as 1000 Hz, which falls above reported temporal pitch limits in cats and humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 draw appropriate conclusions about ferret pitch perception from the behavioral data. Claims C96-C100 discuss an interesting observation about high F0s, acknowledging alternative explanations (C98) while noting that the pattern at lower F0s (C99) supports the temporal cue interpretation. This demonstrates appropriate consideration of alternative hypotheses.

results.result: Primates may be more appropriate models for examining resolved harmonic processing in humans, while ferrets are powerful models for evaluating temporal pitch extraction mechanisms. Like cochlear implant users, ferrets have broad cochlear filters that may limit resolved harmonic cue use.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 appropriately discuss implications for future neurophysiological work. The comparison to cochlear implant users (C103) is insightful and well-supported by the modeling results, suggesting translational relevance of the ferret model.

results.result: The study used appropriate methods including 5 ferrets and 16 humans with power calculations, controlled training procedures, matched stimulus designs across species, and appropriate data analysis procedures including exclusion criteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C125 describe methodological details that are appropriate and well-documented. Power calculations are reported (C104, C105), training procedures are detailed (C109-C115), stimulus design rationale is explained (C113-C114, C121-C123), and analysis procedures are specified (C124-C125). The methods enable replication and support the validity of the results.
